essence: We tested the plan two mock judges liked best: bonds for the cheques and the rest in stocks, with the gift's bottom fixed only in 2031.

Set to promise the same $145,000 in a typical year, it would have to promise under $100,000 about one time in thirteen in our model, ours about one in 150; that costs Laura about $9,000 of her own money in a typical year.
So the draft should answer this rival by name, with both numbers from the same model and the price said out loud, in place of the weaker 60/40 argument.
We argued over what tomorrow's research should chase now that Caplet wants the writing to sound human above everything else.

We've already read a thousand pieces, so tomorrow only goes where we haven't been: people who ask a doubter to pay for a promise in under a hundred words (annuity sellers, auction catalogue writers, mountain guides who set a turn-back time).

Each brings back the writer's real lines with the link and one of our paragraphs rewritten that way, with its numbers and where they came from kept, so the next draft gets better paragraphs, not more notes.
We built the plan two mock judges preferred (bonds for the cheques, the rest in stocks until 2031) and ran it beside ours on the same 200,000 model futures.

Its cheques are just as safe and its gift is about $15,000 bigger on average, but the bottom Laura could promise co-sponsors drops under $100,000 about one time in fifteen to twenty (ours about one in a hundred), nearly always after a stock crash; the extra is simply pay for carrying that crash, and it disappears if stocks earn under about 3% a year.
So the IPS should answer that plan by name of idea, not by rival, in one paragraph that states the price out loud.
We argued over whether owning Laura's gift floor from 2028 costs her about $9,000, as the paragraph said; in our model it is nearer $19,000 on average by 2042, because the rival plan usually wins.

We kept the plan and rewrote the paragraph to say so: the rival usually wins by about $19,000, but in the worst one in twenty markets it has to sell stocks in a slump and names about $90,000 to co-sponsors against our $140,000. Six blind judges preferred that version, and a voice reader ranked it above the plain repair.
The next draft can answer the rival a growth-minded judge would have written, with an honest price, instead of beating a 60/40 four judges called a straw man.

essence: Six fields gave one discipline: sort every dollar by what can fail it, and decide in advance who pays when it does.
The Lab killed our own favourite fix (a 2028 hold-back, $9k of gift) and kept a cheaper one: re-measure the coupon gap in January 2031, before the range is named, for about $160.
The ladder-first structure is what every AI-assisted rival writes; Caplet's edge is the reason (her income can shrink in the same slump), where it breaks, and the two-cost range.

Jun's audit killed two of our own claims: the rising stock share is a bonds-being-spent effect, not a hook, and certainty costs nothing at the median once rivals are matched on misses; its real price is the best years.
We read how twelve real companies work (Pixar, Toyota, Amazon, Netflix and eight more) and argued for four rounds about which habits six busy Year 11s should steal.

Nine passed. The big three: whoever owns a line decides it unless it can't be undone, and then all six vote once; anyone can type "CORD:" to flag a problem at any hour, and the first reply is "thanks"; boring jobs get dealt out on Sundays instead of waiting for a volunteer.

For Caplet: our help on the IPS now gets argued and checked before it reaches you, and the research we found on how teams decide well (some of it from Wharton itself) is yours to use in the Final Report.
